image.description: a quadrilateral whose sides are labeled (1/4*U), (7/4*Q), (2*U), and (8/3*Q).

solution.p: The perimeter is the result from adding the four sides together: {\frac{8}{3}}Q + {\frac{7}{4}}Q + {\frac{1}{4}}U + 2U\text{.} There are two U-terms and two Q-terms. We combine each pair of like terms and the perimeter is {\frac{53}{12}Q+\frac{9}{4}U}\text{.}

image.description: a quadrilateral whose sides are labeled (5/7*B), (7/8*W), (6/5*W), and (4/3*B).

solution.p: The perimeter is the result from adding the four sides together: {\frac{6}{5}}W + {\frac{7}{8}}W + {\frac{5}{7}}B + {\frac{4}{3}}B\text{.} There are two B-terms and two W-terms. We combine each pair of like terms and the perimeter is {\frac{83}{40}W+\frac{43}{21}B}\text{.}

image.description: a quadrilateral whose sides are labeled (k), (c), (c), (2.3*k), (4.9*c), and (78*k).

solution.p: The perimeter is the result from adding the six sides together: c + 2.3k + 4.9c + 78k + k + c\text{.} There are three c-terms and three k-terms. We combine each triple of like terms and the perimeter is {6.9c+81.3k}\text{.}

image.description: a quadrilateral whose sides are labeled (0.1*R), (h), (h), (R), (13*R), and (83*h).

solution.p: The perimeter is the result from adding the six sides together: R + h + 83h + 0.1R + 13R + h\text{.} There are three h-terms and three R-terms. We combine each triple of like terms and the perimeter is {85h+14.1R}\text{.}

image.description: a quadrilateral whose sides are labeled (1/2*c), (5/8*n), (3/2*c), and (3/2*z).

solution.p: The perimeter is the result from adding the six sides together: {\frac{1}{2}}c + {\frac{3}{2}}z + {\frac{5}{3}}z + 4n + {\frac{3}{2}}c + {\frac{5}{8}}n\text{.} There are two n-terms, two z-terms, and two c-terms. We combine each pair of like terms and the perimeter is {\frac{37}{8}n+\frac{19}{6}z+2c}\text{.}

image.description: a quadrilateral whose sides are labeled (3/10*g), (1/3*t), (7/9*z), and (9/8*z).

solution.p: The perimeter is the result from adding the six sides together: {\frac{3}{10}}g + {\frac{9}{8}}z + {\frac{8}{7}}t + {\frac{3}{2}}g + {\frac{7}{9}}z + {\frac{1}{3}}t\text{.} There are two t-terms, two g-terms, and two z-terms. We combine each pair of like terms and the perimeter is {\frac{31}{21}t+\frac{9}{5}g+\frac{137}{72}z}\text{.}

li.p: Let x and y be integers such that x \lt y\text{.}
Then x - y y - x\text{.}

Then xy x + y\text{.}

Then xy x + y\text{.}
Let x and y be integers, such that x \lt y\text{.}

Since x \lt y\text{,} this means that x-y results in a negative number and y-x results in a positive number. Thus, x-y < y-x\text{.}

This problem comes down to looking at the impact of multiplying by y compared to the impact of adding y\text{.} Since x\gt1\text{,} x is at least 2\text{.} Similarly, y is at least 3\text{.} Multiplying by y results in a bigger number than adding y\text{.}

This problem comes down to looking at the impact of multiplying by y compared to the impact of adding y\text{.} Since 0 \lt y \lt 1\text{,} this means that y is a fraction between 0 and 1\text{.} Thus, multiplying by y results in a smaller number, whereas adding y results in a bigger number.
Notice that x + 2y and 2x + y both have an x and a y\text{.} Lets subtract an x and a y from those expressions.
Since y \gt x\text{,} this means that x + 2y \gt 2x + y\text{.}

statement.p: If your restaurant bill is x and you add 20\% tip, the total is x + 0.20x\text{.} If the total was {\$55.56}\text{,} then we have an equation {x+0.2x}={55.56}\text{.} Was the bill before tip {\$46.30}\text{?}

The rental fee for a beach house is a flat {\$310} plus {\$160} per night. So if you stay n nights, the total is {310+160n}\text{.} If the total was {\$1{,}430}\text{,} then we have an equation {310+160n}={1430}\text{.} Did you stay 7 nights?

An elementary school classroom needs a minimum of 120 square feet for the teacher plus a minimum of 36 square feet per student. So if there are n students, the total necessary area is {120+36n} square feet. If a classroom has 768 square feet of area, then we have an inequality {120+36n}\leq{768}\text{.} Could this classroom support 16 students?

[``` 40 = C + 273 ```]
and we need to solve for [`C\text{.}`] With [`273`] being added, we should subtract [`273`] from each side.
[```\newcommand{\subtractright}[1]{{\highlight{{{}-#1}}}}\newcommand{\amp}{&} \begin{aligned} 40\subtractright{273}\amp= C + 273\subtractright{273}\\ -233\amp=C \end{aligned} ```]

This checks out, so the surface temperature of Pluto is [`-233`] degrees Celsius.
END_PGML_SOLUTION

Add four to the number: x + 4
Now double that: 2(x+4)
Then add six: 2(x+4)+6
Then halve it: \frac{2(x + 4)+ 6}{2}
Finally, subtract 7: \frac{2(x + 4)+ 6}{2}-7
This expression can be simplified:
Thus, after following the instructions, you always end up with the original number.

There is no need to solve the equation.

Write an equation where the solution is the amount of time, in hours, that it will take to fill the pool with water. There is no need to solve the equation.

statement.p: To save up for a new phone that costs {\$780}\text{,} Humberto sets aside 1% of his pay each week. This works out to {\$4.12} per week. At present, he has {\$389.50} saved up. How long will it be until Humberto has saved up enough? Write an equation to model this scenario. There is no need to solve it.

A small town would like to replace its aging water treatment system. This will cost {\$8{,}400{,}000}\text{,} but the town just needs {\$1{,}680{,}000} up front for downpayment on a loan that will cover the rest. The town treasury has {\$420{,}000} in it already for this need, and the town can gather {\$140{,}000} per month from taxes. How long will it take to reach enough for downpayment on that loan? Write an equation to model this scenario. There is no need to solve it.

Write an equation to model this scenario. There is no need to solve it.

Serenity baked a pie at 425\,℉ and just took it out of the oven. It immediately starts to cool at a rate of 27\,\frac{℉}{\text{min}}\text{.} How long will it take to cool to 250\,℉\text{?} Write an equation to model this scenario. There is no need to solve it.

On a cold snowy day, the temperature in your home is a cozy 70\,℉\text{,} but then you lose power and heating. Your home temperature begins to drop at a rate of 10\,\frac{℉}{\text{hour}}\text{.} How long will it take before your home is 38\,℉\text{?} Write an equation to model this scenario. There is no need to solve it.

A restaurant stocks its pantry with {100\ {\rm lb}} of onions. When the supply reaches {30\ {\rm lb}}\text{,} its time to order more. Recently, the restaurant has been using {7\ {\rm lb}} of onions per day. How long since restocking will it take until another order must be placed? Write an equation to model this scenario. There is no need to solve it.

At a recent trip to the casino, Danica brought {\$920} in cash. She knows she needs to hold on to {\$100} in reserve to pay for dinner later. Unfortunately Danica had rough luck and was losing money at the slot machines at an average rate of {\$240} per hour. How long was Danica gambling before she had to stop? Write an equation to model this scenario. There is no need to solve it.

For Everetts 8th birthday party, his parents rented a venue that charges a flat fee of {\$90} plus {\$13} per guest. Ultimately it cost Everetts parents {\$350}\text{.} How many guests were there? Write an equation to model this scenario. There is no need to solve it.

Hugos annual property tax had been {\$4{,}905}\text{.} But he did some renovation to his house that added more square footage, and now the annual property tax is {\$5{,}545}\text{.} The county assesses property tax at a rate of {\$2.15} per square foot. solution.p: The interval represents all numbers less than -3\text{.} So in set-builder notation, the interval is {\{ x \mid x \lt -3 \}}\text{.}

And we read the number line from left to right, with the shading extending to -\infty on the left and going all the way up to -3 but not including -3\text{.} So in interval notation, the interval is {\left(-\infty ,-3\right)}\text{.}

image.description: a numberline with a shaded region; the shaded region begins at -1 where there is a left bracket; it extends to the right all the way with an arrowhead

solution.p: The interval represents all numbers greater than or equal to -1\text{.} So in set-builder notation, the interval is {\{ x \mid x \ge -1 \}}\text{.}

And we read the number line from left to right, with the shading starting at -1 (and including -1) and extending on to \infty\text{.} So in interval notation, the interval is {\left[-1,\infty \right)}\text{.}

The set-builder notation tells us to graph all numbers less than or equal to 1\text{.} So the shading can start all the way to the left at -\infty and extend up to 1\text{.} There should be a bracket at 1 to indicate that 1 is included.

And we read the number line from left to right, with the shading extending to -\infty and going all the way up to 1\text{,} including 1\text{.} So in interval notation, the interval is {\left(-\infty ,1\right]}\text{.}

The interval notation tells us to graph all numbers between 2 and \infty\text{.} So the shading can start at 2 and go all the way to the right to \infty. There should be a parenthesis at 2 to indicate that 2 itself is not included.
We have shaded all numbers greater than 2\text{.} So in set-builder notation, the interval is {\{ x \mid x > 2 \}}\text{.}

statement.p: Is {1} a solution to {5x+{\frac{1}{2}}}={3x+{\frac{9}{4}}}\text{?}

solution.p: We have to substitute {1} in for x and simplify each side. The left side simplifies to {{\frac{11}{2}}} and the right side simplifies to {{\frac{21}{4}}}\text{.} Since these are not equal, {1} is not a solution to {5x+{\frac{1}{2}}}={3x+{\frac{9}{4}}}\text{.}

statement.p: Is {7} a solution to {2x+1}\lt{15}\text{?}

solution.p: We have to substitute {7} in for x and simplify each side. The left side simplifies to {15} and the right side simplifies to {15}\text{.} Since {15} is not less than {15}\text{,} {7} is not a solution to {2x+1}={15}\text{.}

statement.p: Find the multiplicative inverse of {-{\frac{1}{7}}}

solution.p: The multiplicative inverse of a negative number will still be negative. The multiplicative inverse of fraction swaps the numerator and denominator. So here the multiplicative inverse of {-{\frac{1}{7}}} is {-7}\text{.}

statement.p: Find the additive inverse of -6

solution.p: The additive inverse of a number is just the negative of that number. So the additive inverse of -6 is 6\text{.}

statement.p: Apply associativity to {{\frac{7}{2}}+\left(q+q^{2}\right)}\text{.}

solution.p: The expression has three terms. To apply associativity, we write the three terms in the same order from left to right, but change which two terms are grouped. This gives us {\left({\frac{7}{2}}+q\right)+q^{2}}\text{.}

statement.p: Apply commutativity of multiplication to {vm+w}\text{.}

solution.p: There is one place in this expression where there is multiplication. To apply commutativity of multiplication, we just write those two factors in the opposite order. This gives us {mv+w}\text{.}

statement.p: Apply the distributive property to {10\mathopen{}\left(B-8\right)}\text{.}

solution.p: The expression has a group of two terms multiplied by 10\text{.} To apply the distributive property, we multiply 10 by each of those two terms. This gives us {10B-10\cdot 8}\text{.}

statement.p: Your savings account starts with \$500\text{.} Then each month, there is an automatic deposit of \$150\text{.} You need \$1700 to afford a deposit on a new apartment. How long will this take?

solution.p: With any word problem, it is best to clearly define the variable you will use once you really understand what the question is asking for. In this case, we let t (for time) be the number of months until you have saved up \$1700\text{.}
To set up an equation, we might start by making a table in order to identify a general pattern for the total amount in the savings account after t months.
We find the pattern is that after t months, the total amount saved is 150t + 500\text{.} Using this pattern, we set up the equation
to represent when we will have saved up \$1700\text{.} To solve this equation, we start by subtracting 500 from each side. Then we can divide each side by 150\text{.}
Checking the solution 8\text{:}
So 8 is the solution, and it checks out. This means it will take 8 months for the account balance to reach \$1700\text{.}

statement.p: Infant Tylenol contains 160 mg of acetaminophen in each 5 mL of liquid. If Baos baby is prescribed 60 mg of acetaminophen, how many milliliters of liquid should he give the baby?

solution.p: Assume Bao should give q milliliters of liquid medicine, so we can set up the following proportion:

p.me: \begin{aligned} \frac{\text{amount of liquid medicine in mL}}{\text{amount of acetaminophen in mg}}\amp=\frac{\text{amount of liquid medicine in mL}}{\text{amount of acetaminophen in mg}}\\ \frac{5\,\text{mL}}{160\,\text{mg}}\amp=\frac{q\,\text{mL}}{60\,\text{mg}}\\ \frac{5}{160}\amp=\frac{q}{60}\\ \multiplyleft{160\cdot 60}\cdot\frac{5}{160}\amp=\multiplyleft{160\cdot 60}\cdot\frac{q}{60}\\ 300\amp=160q\\ \divideunder{300}{160}\amp=\divideunder{160q}{160}\\ q\amp=1.875 \end{aligned}

solution.p: So to give 60 mg of acetaminophen to his baby, Bao should measure out 1.875 mL of the liquid medication.

statement.p: To estimate the health of the Rocky Mountain elk population in the Wenaha Wildlife Area, the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife caught, tagged, and released 33 Rocky Mountain elk. A month later, they returned and observed 43 Rocky Mountain elk, 11 of which had tags. Approximately how many Rocky Mountain elk are in the Wenaha Wildlife Area?

solution.p: Let x represent how many elk are in the Wenaha Wildlife Area. We set up a proportional equation:

p.me: \begin{aligned} \frac{\text{tagged elk}}{\text{total elk}} \amp= \frac{\text{tagged elk}}{\text{total elk}}\\ \frac{11}{43} \amp= \frac{33}{x}\\ \frac{11}{43} \multiplyright{43\cdot x} \amp= \frac{33}{x}\multiplyright{43\cdot x}\\ 11 \cdot x \amp= 33\cdot 43\\ \divideunder{11 \cdot x}{11} \amp= \divideunder{33\cdot 43}{11}\\ x \amp= 129 \end{aligned}

solution.p: There are approximately 129 elk in the Wenaha Wildlife Area.

statement.p: To estimate the health of the black-tailed deer population in the Jewell Meadow Wildlife Area, the Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife caught, tagged, and released 89 black-tailed deer. A month later, they returned and observed 77 black-tailed deer, 12 of which had tags. Approximately how many black-tailed deer are in the Jewell Meadow Wildlife Area?

solution.p: Let x represent how many deer are in the Jewell Meadow Area. We set up a proportional equation:

p.me: \begin{aligned} \frac{\text{tagged deer}}{\text{total deer}} \amp= \frac{\text{tagged deer}}{\text{total deer}}\\ \frac{12}{77} \amp= \frac{89}{x}\\ \frac{12}{77} \multiplyright{77\cdot x} \amp= \frac{89}{x}\multiplyright{77\cdot x}\\ 12 \cdot x \amp= 89\cdot 77\\ \divideunder{12 \cdot x}{12} \amp= \divideunder{89\cdot 77}{12}\\ x \amp= 571 \end{aligned}

solution.p: There are approximately 571 deer in the Jewell Meadow Area.

A month later, they returned and observed 81 black-tailed deer, 10 of which had tags. Approximately how many black-tailed deer are in the Jewell Meadow Wildlife Area?

solution.p: Let x represent how many deer are in the Jewell Meadow Area. We set up a proportional equation:

p.me: \begin{aligned} \frac{\text{tagged deer}}{\text{total deer}} \amp= \frac{\text{tagged deer}}{\text{total deer}}\\ \frac{10}{81} \amp= \frac{95}{x}\\ \frac{10}{81} \multiplyright{81\cdot x} \amp= \frac{95}{x}\multiplyright{81\cdot x}\\ 10 \cdot x \amp= 95\cdot 81\\ \divideunder{10 \cdot x}{10} \amp= \divideunder{95\cdot 81}{10}\\ x \amp= 770 \end{aligned}

solution.p: There are approximately 770 deer in the Jewell Meadow Area.

solution.p: One approach to pattern recognition is to look for a relationship in each row. Here, the y-value in each row is always 10 more than the x-value. So the pattern is described by the equation {y = x+10}\text{.}

statement.p: Write an equation in the form y=\ldots suggested by the pattern in the table.

solution.p: The relationship between x and y in each row is not as clear here. Another popular approach for finding patterns: in each column, consider how the values change from one row to the next. From row to row, the x-value increases by 1\text{.} Also, the y-value increases by 3 from row to row.

Since row-to-row change is always 1 for x and is always 3 for y\text{,} the rate of change from one row to another row is always the same: 3 units of y for every 1 unit of x\text{.} This suggests that y=3x might be a good equation for the table pattern. But if we try to make a table with that pattern:
We find that the values from y=3x are too large by 1\text{.} So now we make an adjustment. The equation {y = 3x-1} describes the pattern in the table.

statement.p: Write an equation in the form y=\ldots suggested by the pattern in the table.

solution.p: Looking for a relationship in each row here, we see that each y-value is the square of the corresponding x-value. That may not be obvious to you. It comes down to recognizing what square numbers are. So the equation is {y = x^{2}}\text{.}
What if we had tried the approach we used in the previous exercise, comparing change from row to row in each column?

Here, the rate of change is not constant from one row to the next. While the x-values are increasing by 1 from row to row, the y-values increase more and more from row to row. Do you notice that there is a pattern there as well? Mathematicians are interested in finding patterns and describing them.

statement.p: What are the slope and y-intercept for each of the following line equations?

solution.p: In the first three equations, simply read the slope m according to slope-intercept form. The slopes are 3.1\text{,} -17\text{,} and {\frac{3}{7}}\text{.}

The fourth equation was written with the terms not in the slope-intercept form order. It could be written y=-8x+13\text{,} and then it is clear that its slope is -8\text{.} In any case, the slope is the coefficient of x\text{.}

The fifth equation is also written with the terms not in the slope-intercept form order. Changing the order of the terms, it could be written y=-\frac{2x}{3}+1\text{,} but this still does not match the pattern of slope-intercept form. Considering how fraction multiplication works, \frac{2x}{3}=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{x}{1}=\frac{2}{3}x\text{.} So we can write this equation as y=-\frac{2}{3}x+1\text{,} and we see the slope is -\frac{2}{3}\text{.}
The last two equations could be written y=2x+0 and y=0x+3\text{,} allowing us to read their slopes as 2 and 0\text{.}

For the y-intercepts, remember that we are expected to answer using an ordered pair (0,b)\text{,} not just a single number b\text{.} We can simply read that the first two y-intercepts are {\left(0,1.78\right)} and {\left(0,112\right)}\text{.}

The third equation does not exactly match the slope-intercept form, until you view it as y=\frac{3}{7}x+\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)\text{,} and then you can see that its y-intercept is \left(0,-\frac{2}{3}\right)\text{.}
With the fourth equation, after rewriting it as y=-8x+13\text{,} we can see that its y-intercept is (0,13)\text{.}
We already explored rewriting the fifth equation as y=-\frac{2}{3}x+1\text{,} where we can see that its y-intercept is (0,1)\text{.}
The last two equations could be written y=2x+0 and y=0x+3\text{,} allowing us to read their y-intercepts as (0,0) and (0,3)\text{.}
Alternatively, we know that y-intercepts happen where x=0\text{,} and substituting x=0 into each equation gives you the y-value of the y-intercept.

statement.p: By your cell phone contract, you pay a monthly fee plus {\$0.06} for each minute you spend on the phone. In one month, you spent 300 minutes over the phone, and had a bill totaling {\$37.00}.

Let x be the number of minutes you spend on the phone in a month, and let y be your total cell phone bill for that month, in dollars. Use a linear equation to model your monthly bill based on the number of minutes you spend on the phone.
This lines slope-intercept equation is .

li.p: A lines equation in slope-intercept form looks like y=mx+b, where m is the slope, and y is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept. The slope of the linear model has been given to us: {\$0.06} per minute.
So now we have that y=0.06x+b. The next step is to find the value of b. There are at least two ways.
One way is to substitute a given point into y={0.06x}+b. We have the point (300,37).

p.m: \begin{aligned} y \amp = {0.06x} + b \\ 37 \amp = 0.06 \cdot 300 + b \\ 37 \amp = 18 + b \\ 37\mathbf{{}-18} \amp = 18 + b\mathbf{{}-18} \\ 19 \amp = b\\ b \amp = 19 \end{aligned}

li.p: This lines slope-intercept equation is y={0.06x}+19.
Another way is to use the lines point-slope equation y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1}). Again, we use the point (300,37).
This is the second way to find b, and thus the lines slope-intercept equation is y=0.06x+19.
In one month, you spent 170 minutes on the phone. To find out the bill, we substitute 170 in for x in the equation y=0.06x+19, and we have:

In one month, you had a cell phone bill of {\$48.40}. To find how many minutes you spent on the phone that month, we substitute 48.4 in for y in the equation y=0.06x+19, and we have:
If your bill was {\$48.40} in one month, you must have spent 490 minutes on the phone.

statement.p: Line S has the equation y = ax + b and Line T has the equation y = cx + d\text{.} Suppose a\gt b\gt c\gt d\gt 0\text{.}

li.p: What can you say about Line S and Line T\text{,} given that a\gt c\text{?} Give as much information about Line S and Line T as possible.
What can you say about Line S and Line T\text{,} given that b\gt d\text{?} Give as much information about Line S and Line T as possible.

Since Line S has the equation y = ax + b and Line T has the equation y =cx + d\text{,} the variables a and c represent slopes. Since a \gt c \gt 0\text{,} we know that the slope of Line S is steeper than the slope of Line T\text{.} We also know that both slopes are positive.

Since Line S has the equation y = ax + b and Line T has the equation y =cx + d\text{,} the variables b and b represent y-intercepts. Since b \gt d \gt 0\text{,} we know that Line S and Line T both intersect the y-axis at positive y-intercepts and that Line S intersects the y-axis at a higher point than Line T\text{.}

introduction.p: Fill in the variables A\text{,} B\text{,} and C in Ax + By = C with the numbers 2, 3 and 13\text{.} You may only use each number once in each part.

statement.p: For the steepest possible slope, A must be , B must be , and C must be .

solution.p: Lets put Ax + By = C into slope-intercept form. Then, the equation becomes y = \frac{-A}{B}x + \frac{C}{B}\text{.} To make the steepest slope possible, we must maximize the fraction \frac{A}{B}\text{.} The possibilities are \frac{2}{3}\text{,} \frac{2}{13}\text{,} \frac{3}{2}\text{,} \frac{3}{13}\text{,} \frac{13}{2}\text{,} and \frac{13}{3}\text{.} The biggest of these is \frac{13}{2}\text{.} Thus, A must equal 13, B must equal 2, and C must equal 3.

statement.p: For the shallowest possible slope, A must be , B must be , and C must be .

solution.p: To make the shallowest slope possible, we must minimize the fraction \frac{A}{B}\text{.} The smallest of the possible fractions is \frac{2}{13}\text{.} Thus, A must equal 2, B must equal 13, and C must equal 3.

li.p: A lines equation in slope-intercept form looks like y=mx+b, where m is the slope, and y is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept. The slope of the linear model has been given to us: {\$0.04} per minute.
So now we have that y=0.04x+b. The next step is to find the value of b. There are at least two ways.
One way is to substitute a given point into y={0.04x}+b. We have the point (270,28.8).

p.m: \begin{aligned} y \amp = {0.04x} + b \\ 28.8 \amp = 0.04 \cdot 270 + b \\ 28.8 \amp = 10.8 + b \\ 28.8\mathbf{{}-10.8} \amp = 10.8 + b\mathbf{{}-10.8} \\ 18 \amp = b\\ b \amp = 18 \end{aligned}

li.p: This lines slope-intercept equation is y={0.04x}+18.
Another way is to use the lines point-slope equation y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1}). Again, we use the point (270,28.8).
This is the second way to find b, and thus the lines slope-intercept equation is y=0.04x+18.

If your bill was {\$34.80} in one month, you must have spent 420 minutes on the phone.

li.p: A lines equation in slope-intercept form looks like y=mx+b, where m is the slope, and y is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept. Since the gas is leaking at a rate of 5 grams per minute, we know that the slope of the linear model is -5.
So now we have that y=-5x+b. The next step is to find the value of b. There are at least two ways.
One way is to substitute a known point into y=-5x+b. We use the point (5,195).

p.m: \begin{aligned} y \amp = -5x + b \\ 195 \amp = -5 \cdot 5 + b \\ 195 \amp = -25 + b \\ 195\mathbf{{} + 25} \amp = -25 + b\mathbf{{} + 25} \\ 220 \amp = b\\ b \amp = 220 \end{aligned}

li.p: This lines slope-intercept equation is y=-5x+220.
Another way is to use the lines point-slope equation y-y_{1}=m(x-x_{1}). Again, we use the point (5,195).

p.m: \begin{aligned} y-y_{1} \amp = m(x-x_{1}) \\ y-195 \amp = -5(x-5) \\ y-195 \amp = -5x - 5 \cdot (-5) \\ y-195 \amp = -5x+25 \\ y-195\mathbf{{}+195} \amp = -5x+25\mathbf{{}+195} \\ y \amp = -5x+220 \end{aligned}

li.p: This is the second way to find b, and thus the lines slope-intercept equation is y=-5x+220.
After 32 minutes, we can find the mass of the remaining gas if we substitute 32 in for x in the equation y=-5x+220. We have:
So after 32 minutes, there are 60 grams of gas remaining.
To find when the gas will be all gone, we need to find when there are 0 grams of gas left. We can substitute 0 in for y in the equation y=-5x+220, and we have:
So after 44 minutes, the gas will be all gone.

introduction.p: Cohen is organizing an office lunch party. His budget for beverages is {\$54} and he will try to spend all of it. He assumes that 12 people will attend, and there should be two beverages available per person. Cohen has decided to order cans of a fancy beverage that cost {\$3} each, and cans of a cheaper beverage that cost {\$2}each. How many of each should he order?

statement.p: Write two equations that form a system for this scenario.

solution.p: Since there are 12 people and there should be two drinks per person, one equation is {3x+2y = 54}\text{.}
Since the first type costs {\$3} each, the second type costs {\$2} each, and the total should be {\$54}\text{,} another equation is {x+y = 24}\text{.}

statement.p: Plot the lines for the system of two equations.

solution.p: Plotting the two slope-intercept equations:

image.description: a Cartesian grid with two intersecting lines; one line passes through (0,54/2) and (54/3,0); the other line passes through (0,2*12) and (2*12,0); the lines cross at (6,18)

statement.p: Based on the graph, how many of the more expensive beverage should Cohen buy?
How many of the less expensive beverage should Cohen buy?

solution.p: The lines cross at (6,18)\text{.} So Cohen should buy 6 of the more expensive drink, and 18 of the less expensive drink.

introduction.p: At the local hardware store, Lauren bought a hammer and two boxes of nails. The total cost was {\$16}\text{.} The hammer costs {\$7} more than a box of nails. How much does a hammer cost and how much does one box of nails cost?

statement.p: Write two equations that form a system for this scenario.

solution.p: Since the total cost of the hammer and two boxes of nails is {\$16}\text{,} one equation is {x+2y = 16}\text{.}
Since the hammer costs {\$7} more than a box of nails, another equation is {x = y+7}\text{.}

statement.p: Plot the lines for the system of two equations.

solution.p: Plotting the two slope-intercept equations:

image.description: a Cartesian grid with two intersecting lines; one line passes through (0,16/2) and (16,0); the other line passes through (0,-7) and (7,0); the lines cross at (10,3)

statement.p: Based on the graph, how much does the hammer cost?
How much does a box of nails cost?

solution.p: The lines cross at (10,3)\text{.} So a hammer costs {\$10}\text{,} and a box of nails costs $3.

introduction.p: Alia enters a grassy field from some dense trees. Her dog is standing out in the field, {110\ {\rm ft}} away. As soon as they see each other, they start running toward each other. Alia runs with speed {3\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut m}{\rm\mathstrut s}}} and her dog runs with speed {8\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut m}{\rm\mathstrut s}}}\text{.} How long will it be until they meet?

statement.p: Write two equations that form a system for this scenario.

solution.p: Alia starts out at position d=0\text{,} running with speed {3\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut m}{\rm\mathstrut s}}}\text{.} So one equation is {d = 3t}\text{.}

The dog starts running with speed {8\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut m}{\rm\mathstrut s}}} but getting closer to Alia. So well use a negative rate of change. And the dog starts out {110\ {\rm ft}} away. So the other equation is {d = 110+\left(-8\right)t}\text{.}

statement.p: Plot the lines for the system of two equations.

solution.p: Plotting the two slope-intercept equations:

image.description: a Cartesian grid with two intersecting lines; one line passes through (0,110) with slope 3; the other line passes through (0,0) with slope -8; the lines cross at (10,30)

statement.p: Based on the graph, how long will it be until they meet?
How far will that be from the place where Alia started?

solution.p: The lines cross at (10,30)\text{.} So after 10 seconds, they will meet 30 feet away from where Alia started.

introduction.p: A cyclist riding at {30\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut ft}{\rm\mathstrut s}}} rides past a dog. A moment later, when the bicycle is {40\ {\rm ft}} away, the dog begins to chase the bicycle at a speed of {35\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut ft}{\rm\mathstrut s}}}\text{.} Assuming the cyclist does not change course or speed, how long will it be until the dog catches up to the bicycle?

statement.p: Write two equations that form a system for this scenario.

solution.p: The bicycle starts out {40\ {\rm ft}} away and is traveling at {30\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut ft}{\rm\mathstrut s}}}\text{.} So one equation is {d = 30t+40}\text{.}
The dog starts running at time t=0 with speed {35\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut ft}{\rm\mathstrut s}}}\text{.} So the other equation is {d = 35t}\text{.}

statement.p: Plot the lines for the system of two equations.

solution.p: Plotting the two slope-intercept equations:

image.description: a Cartesian grid with two intersecting lines; one line passes through (0,40) with slope 30; the other line passes through (0,0) with slope 35; the lines cross at (8,280)

statement.p: Based on the graph, how long will it be until the dog catches up with the bicycle?
How far will that be from the place where the dog started running?

solution.p: The lines cross at (8,280)\text{.} So after 8 seconds, the cyclist and the dog are each 280 feet away from where the dog started running.

introduction.p: Desi owns a coffee shop and they want to mix two different types of coffee beans to make a blend that sells for \$12.50 per pound. They have some coffee beans from Columbia that sell for \$9.00 per pound and some coffee beans from Honduras that sell for \$14.00 per pound. How many pounds of each should they mix to make 30 pounds of the blend?

statement.p: Write two equations that form a system for this scenario.

solution.p: We have C pounds of Columbian coffee and H pounds of Honduran coffee. Since there must be 30 pounds total, one equation is C+H=30\text{.}

The total cost of the Colombian coffee in the blend will be 9C\text{,} and the total cost of the Honduran coffee in the blend will be 14H\text{.} All together, the blend has a total cost of 12.50\cdot30=375 dollars. So another equation is 9C+14H=375\text{.}

statement.p: Isolate one of the variables in one of the equations.

solution.p: We choose to isolate C in the first equation. All we need to do subtract H from each side, and then C = 30 - H\text{.}

statement.p: Substitute the isolated expression into the other equation.

solution.p: Making the substitution: 9(30 - H) + 14H = 375\text{.}

statement.p: Solve this equation in one variable and then solve for the other variable using the isolation from a previous step. Finally, report how much of each type of coffee Desi should use.

solution.p: In summary, Desi needs to mix 21 pounds of the Honduran coffee beans with 9 pounds of the Columbian coffee beans to create this blend.

introduction.p: Practice adding when at least one negative number is involved. The expectation is that you can do these tasks without a calculator.

statement.p: Add -1+9\text{.}

solution.p: The two numbers have opposite sign, so we subtract 9-1=8\text{.} Of the two numbers being added, the positive is larger, so the result should positive as well: 8\text{.}
The two numbers are both negative, so we can add 12+98=110\text{,} and take the negative of that as the answer: -110\text{.}
The two numbers have opposite sign, so we subtract 123-100=23\text{.} Of the two numbers being added, the negative is larger, so the result should be negative: -23\text{.}

statement.p: Find the sum -2.1+(-2.1)\text{.}

solution.p: The two numbers are both negative, so we can add 2.1+2.1=4.2\text{,} and take the negative of that as the answer: -4.2\text{.}

statement.p: Find the sum -34.67+81.53\text{.}

solution.p: The two numbers have opposite sign, so we can subtract 81.53-34.67=46.86\text{.} Of the two numbers being added, the positive is larger, so the result should be positive: 46.86\text{.}

introduction.p: Practice subtracting when at least one negative number is involved. The expectation is that you can do these tasks without a calculator.

statement.p: Subtract -1 from 9\text{.}

solution.p: After writing this as 9-(-1)\text{,} we can change to 9+1 and get 10\text{.}

statement.p: Subtract 32-50\text{.}

solution.p: We can change this to 32+(-50)\text{.} Two numbers are added, and the larger one is negative. So we find the difference 50-32=18\text{,} but the final result must be negative: -18\text{.}

statement.p: Subtract 108-(-108)\text{.}

solution.p: We can rewrite this as 108+108 and get 216\text{.}

statement.p: Find the difference -5.9-(-3.1)\text{.}

solution.p: We can rewrite this as -5.9+3.1\text{.} Now it is the sum of two numbers of opposite sign, so we find the difference 5.9-3.1=2.8\text{.} We were adding two numbers where the larger one was negative. So the final result should also be negative: -2.8\text{.}

statement.p: Find the difference -12.04-17.2\text{.}

solution.p: Since we are subtracting a positive number from a negative number, the result should be an even more negative number. We can add 12.04+17.2 to get 29.24\text{,} but our final answer should be the opposite, -29.24\text{.}

introduction.p: Here are some practice exercises with multiplication and signed numbers. The expectation is that you can make these calculations without a calculator.

statement.p: Multiply -13\cdot2\text{.}

solution.p: Since 13\cdot2=26\text{,} and we are multiplying numbers of opposite signs, the answer is negative: -26\text{.}

statement.p: Find the product of 30 and -50\text{.}

solution.p: Since 30\cdot50=1500\text{,} and we are multiplying numbers of opposite signs, the answer is negative: -1500\text{.}

statement.p: Compute -12(-7)\text{.}

solution.p: Since 12\cdot7=84\text{,} and we are multiplying numbers of the same sign, the answer is positive: 84\text{.}

statement.p: Find the product -285(0)\text{.}

solution.p: Any number multiplied by 0 is 0\text{.}

introduction.p: Here is some practice with natural exponents on negative bases. The expectation is that YOU can make these calculations without a calculator.

statement.p: Compute (-8)^2\text{.}

solution.p: Since 8^2 is 64 and we are raising a negative number to an even power, the answer is positive: 64\text{.}

statement.p: Calculate the power (-1)^{203}\text{.}

solution.p: Since 1^{203} is 1 and we are raising a negative number to an odd power, the answer is negative: -1\text{.}

statement.p: Find (-3)^3\text{.}

solution.p: Since 3^{3} is 27 and we are raising a negative number to an odd power, the answer is negative: -27\text{.}

statement.p: Calculate -5^2\text{.}

solution.p: Be careful: here we are raising positive 5 to the second power to get 25 and then negating the result: -25\text{.}
Here are two different explanations of how two negative numbers can be added together.
METHOD 1
Use a number line. Lets find -10+(-3).
First, find -10 on the number line. Next, since we are adding a negative number, we move left, in the negative direction, by 3 units. We will reach {-13} on the number line, which is the answer.
METHOD 2
A second method asks you to think in terms of money. Lets find -10+(-3).
The first number is -10. Since its negative, its like you lost 10 dollars while gambling at the casino this morning.
The second number is -3. Since its negative, its like you lost 3 dollars again while gambling in the casino this afternoon.
Since you lost twice, you ended up losing a lot, implying the answer is negative.
Since you lost 10 dollars and then lost 3 dollars, it makes sense that you lost a total of {13} dollars. So the final answer is: -10+(-3)={-13}.

When two negative numbers are multiplied together they make a positive number; each pair of negative signs cancel each other out.
When an odd number of negative numbers are multiplied together, each pair of negative signs cancel out but there is still one negative sign left. Thats why (-1)^{\text{odd number}}=-1.
Similarly, when an even number of negative numbers are multiplied together each pair of negative signs cancel out and there are no negative signs left. Thats why (-1)^{\text{even number}}=1.

introduction.p: Select the correct word to make each statement true.

statement.p:
A positive number minus a positive number is
?
sometimes
always
never negative.

solution.p: A positive number minus a positive number is sometimes negative. For example, consider 6 - 3 = 3 and consider 6 - 8 = -2\text{.}

statement.p:
A negative number plus a negative number is
?
sometimes
always
never negative.

solution.p: A negative number plus a negative number is always negative.

statement.p:
A positive number minus a negative number is
?
sometimes
always
never positive.

solution.p: A positive number minus a negative number is always positive.

statement.p:
A negative number multiplied by a negative number is
?
sometimes
always
never negative.

solution.p: A negative number multiplied by a negative number is never negative. A negative number multiplied by a negative number is always positive.

Alexis sells cars for a living, and earns 28\% of the dealerships sales profit as commission. In a certain month, she plans to earn \$2200 in commissions. How much total sales profit does she need to bring in for the dealership?
Alexis needs to bring in in sales profit.

solution.p: Be careful that you do not calculate 28\% of \$2200\text{.} That might be what a student would do who doesnt thoroughly read the question. If you have ever trained yourself to quickly find numbers in word problems and substitute them into formulas, you must unlearn this. The issue is that \$2200 is not the dealerships sales profit, and if you mistakenly multiply 0.28\cdot2200=616\text{,} then \$616 makes no sense as an answer to this question. How could Alexis bring in only \$616 of sales profit, and earn \$2200 in commission?
We can translate the problem into \$2200 is 28\% of what? Letting x be the sales profit for the dealership (in dollars), we can write and solve the equation:
To earn \$2200 in commission, Alexis needs to bring in approximately \$7857.14 of sales profit for the dealership.

BEGIN_PGML Alexis sells cars for a living, and earns [`28\%`] of the dealership's sales profit as commission. In a certain month, she plans to earn [`\$2200`] in commissions. How much total sales profit does she need to bring in for the dealership?
Alexis needs to bring in [_]{$sales}{10} in sales profit.
END_PGML
############################################################ # Solution ############################################################
BEGIN_PGML_SOLUTION Be careful that you do not calculate [`28\%`] of [`\$2200\text{.}`] That might be what a student would do who doesn't thoroughly read the question. If you have ever trained yourself to quickly find numbers in word problems and substitute them into formulas, you must _unlearn_ this. The issue is that [`\$2200`] is not the dealership's sales profit, and if you mistakenly multiply [`0.28\cdot2200=616\text{,}`] then [`\$616`] makes no sense as an answer to this question. How could Alexis bring in only [`\$616`] of sales profit, and earn [`\$2200`] in commission?
We can translate the problem into "[`\$2200`] is [`28\%`] of what?" Letting [`x`] be the sales profit for the dealership (in dollars), we can write and solve the equation:
[```\newcommand{\pinover}[2]{\overset{\overset{\mathrm{\ #2\ }}{|}}{\strut #1 \strut}}\newcommand{\divideunder}[2]{\frac{#1}{{\highlight{{#2}}}}}\newcommand{\amp}{&} \begin{aligned} \pinover{2200}{\$2200}\amp\pinover{=}{is}\pinover{0.28}{28\%}\pinover{\cdot}{of}\pinover{x}{what}\\ \divideunder{2200}{0.28}\amp=\divideunder{0.28x}{0.28}\\ 7857.14\amp\approx x\\ x\amp\approx7857.14 \end{aligned} ```]
To earn [`\$2200`] in commission, Alexis needs to bring in approximately [`\$7857.14`] of sales profit for the dealership.
END_PGML_SOLUTION
############################################################ # End Problem ############################################################
ENDDOCUMENT();

li.p: Give an example of a whole number that is not an integer.
Give an example of an integer that is not a whole number.
Give an example of a rational number that is not an integer.
Give an example of a irrational number.
Give an example of a irrational number that is also an integer.
Since all whole numbers belong to integers, we cannot write any whole number which is not an integer. Type DNE (does not exist) for this question.
Any negative integer, like -1, is not a whole number, but is an integer.
Any terminating decimal, like 1.2, is a rational number, but is not an integer.
\pi is the easiest number to remember as an irrational number. Another constant worth knowing is e\approx2.718. Finally, the square root of most integers are irrational, like \sqrt{2} and \sqrt{3}.
All irrational numbers are non-repeating and non-terminating decimals. No irrational numbers are integers.

Which of the following are whole numbers? There may be more than one correct answer.

solution.p: To be a whole number, you have to be one of the numbers 0,1,2,\ldots. Sometimes whole numbers are explicitly written this way, and sometimes they are hidden. For example \sqrt{4} is a whole number, since \sqrt{4}=2. So the correct answers are BE.

statement.p: Which of the following are integers? There may be more than one correct answer.

solution.p: To be an integer, you have to be one of the numbers \ldots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\ldots. Sometimes integers are explicitly written this way, and sometimes they are hidden. For example \sqrt{4} is an integer, since \sqrt{4}=2. So the correct answers are ABEG.

solution.p: To be an integer, you have to be one of the numbers \ldots,-2,-1,0,1,2,\ldots. Sometimes integers are explicitly written this way, and sometimes they are hidden. For example \sqrt{4} is an integer, since \sqrt{4}=2. So the correct answers are BDFH.

statement.p: Which of the following are rational numbers? There may be more than one correct answer.

solution.p: To be an rational number, you either have to be a fraction with whole numbers for the numerator and denominator, or you have to be a number with a terminating decimal expression, or you have to be a number with a repeating decimal expression. (Actually, these descriptions are a little redundant.) Sometimes rational numbers are explicitly written in one of these ways, and sometimes they are hidden. For example \sqrt{0.16} is a rational number, since \sqrt{0.16}=0.4. So the correct answers are ABCEGH.

(Actually, these descriptions are a little redundant.) Sometimes rational numbers are explicitly written in one of these ways, and sometimes they are hidden. For example \sqrt{0.16} is a rational number, since \sqrt{0.16}=0.4. So the correct answers are CDEFGH.

statement.p: Which of the following are irrational numbers? There may be more than one correct answer.

solution.p: To be an irrational number, you simply have to not be a rational number. A rational number is a number that can be written as a fraction with whole numbers for the numerator and denominator, or with a terminating decimal expression, or with a repeating decimal expression. (Actually, these descriptions are a little redundant.) Sometimes rational numbers are explicitly written in one of these ways, and sometimes they are hidden. For example \sqrt{0.16} is a rational number, since \sqrt{0.16}=0.4. The irrational numbers here are are FG.

For example \sqrt{0.16} is a rational number, since \sqrt{0.16}=0.4. The irrational numbers here are are AG.

li.p: Give an example of a whole number that is not an integer.
Give an example of an integer that is not a whole number.
Give an example of a rational number that is not an integer.
Give an example of a irrational number.
Give an example of a irrational number that is also an integer.
Since all whole numbers belong to integers, we cannot write any whole number which is not an integer. Type DNE (does not exist) for this question.
Any negative integer, like -1, is not a whole number, but is an integer.
Any terminating decimal, like 1.2, is a rational number, but is not an integer.
\pi is the easiest number to remember as an irrational number. Another constant worth knowing is e\approx2.718. Finally, the square root of most integers are irrational, like \sqrt{2} and \sqrt{3}.
All irrational numbers are non-repeating and non-terminating decimals. No irrational numbers are integers.

Imagine making up a number with the following pattern. After the decimal point, write the natural numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, etc. The decimal digits will extend forever with this pattern: 0.12345\ldots\text{.}

Is the number a rational number or an irrational number?
?
rational
irrational

solution.p: The number is irrational. The decimal will never end and it will never repeat.
